questions.q: Froth flotation is used for the concentration of:
questions.solution:
**Froth flotation** concentrates **sulphide** ores, exploiting the fact that sulphide particles are **preferentially wetted by oil** while the gangue is wetted by water.

Pine oil acts as the collector and sodium ethyl xanthate as the frothing agent. The ore floats with the froth and is skimmed off.

Oxide ores are concentrated by **gravity separation** or **magnetic separation**, and bauxite specifically by the chemical **Bayer process**.

An Ellingham diagram plots the standard free energy of formation $\Delta G^\circ$ of metal oxides **against temperature**.

Its practical use is in choosing a **reducing agent**: a metal whose line lies **below** another's can reduce that other metal's oxide, because the overall $\Delta G$ is then negative.

Most lines slope **upward** because $\Delta S$ is negative when a gas is consumed. The carbon line slopes **downward**, since $\text{C} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{CO}$ increases the number of gas molecules — which is exactly why carbon becomes a better reducing agent at high temperature and why it reduces almost any oxide if heated enough.

questions.q: The metal extracted by Hall-Heroult process is :
questions.solution:
The Hall-Heroult process is the electrolysis of pure alumina dissolved in molten cryolite, $\mathrm{Na_3AlF_6}$, which lowers the melting point and raises the conductivity.

Aluminium is liberated at the carbon cathode: **Al**.

questions.q: Zone refining is based on the principle that:
options: Impurities are more soluble in the molten state than in the solid
questions.solution:
**Zone refining** works because impurities are **more soluble in the molten metal than in the solid**.

A mobile heater melts a narrow band, which is moved slowly along the rod. The impurities travel with the molten zone and collect at one end, which is then cut off.

It produces metals of **very high purity** and is used for silicon and germanium in semiconductor manufacture, where the tolerance for impurity is a few parts per billion.

questions.q: Extraction of gold and silver involves leaching with cyanide ion. Silver is later recovered by :
questions.solution:
Leaching dissolves silver as the complex $[\mathrm{Ag(CN)_2}]^-$. Zinc is more electropositive and **displaces** the silver:

$2[\mathrm{Ag(CN)_2}]^- + \mathrm{Zn} \rightarrow [\mathrm{Zn(CN)_4}]^{2-} + 2\mathrm{Ag}$

questions.q: The essential difference between roasting and calcination is that roasting is carried out:
options: In the presence of excess air
questions.solution:
**Roasting** heats the ore **in the presence of excess air**, and is used for **sulphide** ores, converting them to oxides and driving off $\text{SO}_2$.

**Calcination** heats the ore in the **absence or limited supply of air**, and is used for **carbonate and hydrated** ores, driving off $\text{CO}_2$ or water.

Both end at the oxide, because the oxide is what carbon or another reducing agent can then reduce to the metal. The difference is only in what has to be removed to get there.

questions.q: In the van Arkel process, the metal is purified by:
options: Forming a volatile compound that is later decomposed on a hot filament
questions.solution:
The **van Arkel process** converts the metal into a **volatile compound**, which is then decomposed on a hot tungsten filament to deposit the pure metal.

For titanium and zirconium:

$\text{Ti} + 2\text{I}_2 \xrightarrow{250^\circ\text{C}} \text{TiI}_4 \xrightarrow{1400^\circ\text{C}} \text{Ti} + 2\text{I}_2$

The iodine is recycled. The method is valuable because it removes **oxygen and nitrogen** as impurities, which other methods struggle with — and those are exactly the impurities that make titanium brittle.

questions.q: In the blast furnace, limestone is added to:
options: Act as a flux, removing silica as slag
questions.solution:
Limestone decomposes to lime, which acts as a **basic flux** and combines with the acidic silica impurity to form a fusible **slag**:

$\text{CaCO}_3 \rightarrow \text{CaO} + \text{CO}_2$

$\text{CaO} + \text{SiO}_2 \rightarrow \text{CaSiO}_3$ (slag)

The slag is lighter than molten iron and floats on it, so the two are tapped off separately. It also protects the metal from re-oxidation.

The **reduction** is done by carbon monoxide, not by limestone.

questions.q: Aluminium is used to reduce the oxides of chromium and manganese because:
options: It is a stronger reducing agent than carbon for these oxides
It has a lower melting point
questions.solution:
In the **thermite (Goldschmidt) reaction**, aluminium reduces oxides such as $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_3$ and $\text{Mn}_3\text{O}_4$.

On the Ellingham diagram the aluminium line lies **below** those of chromium and manganese, so the reduction has a negative $\Delta G$ and proceeds.

Carbon is avoided here for a practical reason rather than a thermodynamic one: at the temperatures needed, carbon would form **carbides** with these metals, contaminating the product. The thermite reaction is also strongly exothermic, which is why it is used for welding rails in place.

questions.q: What is the oxidation state of aluminium in $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$?
questions.solution:
Oxygen is $-2$ each and there are three of them, giving $-6$. Let aluminium be $x$ each.

$2x + 3(-2) = 0$

$2x = 6 \Rightarrow x = \mathbf{+3}$

questions.q: In the reaction $\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 + 3\text{CO} \rightarrow 2\text{Fe} + 3\text{CO}_2$, how many moles of CO are needed per mole of iron produced?
questions.solution:
The equation gives 3 moles of CO for 2 moles of Fe.

Per mole of iron: $\dfrac{3}{2} = \mathbf{1.5}$ moles of CO.

questions.q: How many faradays of charge are required to deposit 1 mole of aluminium from $\text{Al}^{3+}$?
questions.solution:
$\text{Al}^{3+} + 3e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Al}$

Three moles of electrons are needed per mole of aluminium, so $\mathbf{3}$ faradays, or $3 \times 96500 = 289500\ \text{C}$.

This large charge requirement is precisely why aluminium extraction is so energy-intensive, and why recycling aluminium uses only about $5\%$ of the energy of extracting it.

questions.q: In the electrolytic refining of copper, which one of the following is used as anode ?
questions.solution:
The **impure copper** is the anode and dissolves as $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$; pure copper is deposited on a thin pure-copper cathode.

Less reactive impurities such as silver and gold fall below the anode as anode mud; more reactive ones stay in solution.

questions.q: What is the oxidation state of sulphur in the sulphide ion $\text{S}^{2-}$?
questions.solution:
A monatomic ion's oxidation state equals its charge, so sulphur is $\mathbf{-2}$.

Roasting oxidises it to $+4$ in $\text{SO}_2$, which is a change of six units — a substantial oxidation, and the reason roasting releases so much heat.

questions.q: Explain the principle and uses of the Ellingham diagram. Use it to explain why carbon is an effective reducing agent at high temperatures, why aluminium is used in the thermite reaction, and state two limitations of the diagram.
questions.solution:
**What the diagram is.** An Ellingham diagram plots the standard free energy change $\Delta G^\circ$ for the formation of metal **oxides** against **temperature**, for reactions written per mole of oxygen consumed:

$2\text{M} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MO}$

Writing them per mole of $\text{O}_2$ is what makes the lines directly comparable.

**Why most lines slope upward.** From $\Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ$, the slope of each line is $-\Delta S^\circ$.

For most oxidations a gas ($\text{O}_2$) is consumed and a solid formed, so $\Delta S^\circ$ is **negative**, the slope $-\Delta S^\circ$ is **positive**, and the line rises. Oxide formation becomes **less** favourable as temperature rises.

**The principle of use.** A metal can reduce the oxide of another metal if its own line lies **below** that oxide's line at the working temperature, because the coupled reaction then has a negative $\Delta G$.

The vertical gap between the two lines is the $\Delta G$ of the reduction, so a larger gap means a stronger driving force.

**Why carbon works so well at high temperature.** Carbon is the important exception, and the reason is its entropy.

Three carbon reactions matter:

$\text{C} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{CO}_2$ — one mole of gas to one mole, so $\Delta S \approx 0$ and the line is roughly **horizontal**.

$2\text{C} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{CO}$ — one mole of gas becomes **two**, so $\Delta S$ is **positive** and the line slopes **downward**.

$2\text{CO} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{CO}_2$ — three moles to two, so the line rises steeply.

The $\text{CO}$ line falling while every metal oxide line rises means the two must **cross**. Above the crossing temperature carbon lies below the metal's line and can reduce its oxide.

**This is the key insight of the whole diagram**: carbon becomes a **better** reducing agent the hotter it gets, while metals become worse. Given a high enough temperature, carbon will reduce almost any metal oxide — which is why carbon is the cheap industrial reductant of choice, used in the blast furnace for iron and for zinc, tin and lead.

**Why aluminium is used in the thermite reaction.** The aluminium line lies **very low** on the diagram, below those of chromium, manganese and iron, so aluminium can reduce their oxides:

$\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_3 + 2\text{Al} \rightarrow 2\text{Cr} + \text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$

The large gap between the lines means a large negative $\Delta G$, and the reaction is strongly **exothermic** — hot enough to produce molten metal, which is why thermite is used to weld railway rails in place.

Carbon is avoided here not because it could not reduce these oxides thermodynamically, but for a practical reason: at the temperatures required, carbon forms **carbides** with chromium and manganese, contaminating the product. The diagram tells you what is possible; it does not tell you what is clean.

**Two limitations.**

**1. It says nothing about rate.** Ellingham diagrams are built entirely on **thermodynamics**. A reduction the diagram shows as feasible may proceed immeasurably slowly, because $\Delta G$ says nothing about activation energy. Feasible and practical are different questions.

**2. It assumes reactants and products are in their standard states, at unit activity.** Real processes involve alloys, solutions and varying partial pressures, so the actual $\Delta G$ departs from $\Delta G^\circ$. The diagram also assumes the reactants are in equilibrium, which a flowing industrial furnace is not.

A third worth knowing is that it gives no information about **side reactions** — exactly the carbide formation that rules carbon out for chromium, which the diagram itself cannot warn you about.
